item.title: Joseph Schooling's Journey: From Childhood Dream to Singapore's First Olympic Gold
item.description: How family sacrifice, American training and an Olympic record over Michael Phelps shaped the life of Singapore's greatest swimmer.
item.content:encoded:
On 12 August 2016, 21-year-old Joseph Isaac Schooling entered lane four at the Olympic Aquatics Stadium in Rio de Janeiro and stopped the clock in 50.39 seconds. That swim took 0.19 seconds off Michael Phelps's 2008 Olympic record, forced Phelps, Chad le Clos and László Cseh into an unprecedented three-way tie for silver at 51.14 seconds, and delivered Singapore's first and only Olympic gold medal. Born on 16 June 1995 to Colin and May Schooling, the fourth-generation Singaporean had pursued that specific wall touch since boyhood, tracing a lineage of Olympic ambition that began almost seven decades earlier.

Schooling's Olympic motivation originated with his grand-uncle Lloyd Valberg, a high jumper who competed at the 1948 London Games as Singapore's first Olympian. Schooling was raised in Singapore as the only child in a sporting household: his father Colin, educated at Raffles Institution, represented Singapore in softball after competing in water polo and hurdles, while his mother May had played professional tennis in Malaysia before moving from Perak. After attending Anglo-Chinese School (Junior) and Anglo-Chinese School (Independent), Schooling met Phelps in Singapore in 2008 when the American stopped over ahead of the Beijing Games. A photograph captured the 13-year-old Singaporean standing beside his swimming idol.

Determined to pursue world-class competition, Schooling left Singapore in 2009 at age 14 to attend the Bolles School in Jacksonville, Florida, training under Spanish Olympic medallist Sergio López Miró. The relocation required significant financial and family sacrifice. Colin and May Schooling sold a residential property in Australia and spent more than S$1 million to finance their son's coaching, schooling and living costs, alternating shifts between Jacksonville and Singapore to run their business while supporting him.

From London Heartbreak to Asian Games Glory

Schooling earned his first Olympic "A" qualifying standard at the 2011 Southeast Asian Games in Palembang, winning the 200m butterfly in 1:56.67. His Olympic debut at the 2012 London Games, however, ended in disappointment. Minutes before his 200m butterfly heat at the London Aquatics Centre, swimming officials rejected his swim cap and goggles for non-compliance with equipment rules. Forced to scramble for replacements before the buzzer, Schooling clocked 2:01.31, finished 26th overall, and missed the semi-finals.

The setback launched an accelerated climb. In July 2014, Schooling became Singapore's first swimming medallist at the Commonwealth Games, securing silver in the 100m butterfly in Glasgow. Two months later at the Incheon Asian Games, he won bronze in the 200m butterfly, silver in the 50m butterfly, and gold in the 100m butterfly with a Games record of 51.76 seconds, ending a 32-year title drought for Singapore's male swimmers. Later that year, he enrolled at the University of Texas at Austin to swim for Hall of Fame coaches Eddie Reese and Kris Kubik. In June 2015, Schooling collected nine gold medals and nine Games records at the Southeast Asian Games on home soil, clocking 22.47 seconds in the 50m freestyle to erase Ang Peng Siong's 33-year-old national record. Two months later at the Kazan World Championships, he took bronze in the 100m butterfly with an Asian-record time of 50.96 seconds, securing Singapore's first world aquatics medal.

The Rio Pinnacle and Collegiate Supremacy

Schooling arrived at the Rio 2016 Olympics following a dominant collegiate run for the Texas Longhorns, where he set NCAA and US Open records of 44.01 seconds in the 100-yard butterfly and 1:37.97 in the 200-yard butterfly. In Rio's 100m butterfly semi-finals on 11 August, he qualified fastest in an Asian record of 50.83 seconds. In the final on 12 August, Schooling opened with a split of 23.64 seconds at the halfway mark before finishing in 50.39 seconds, beating Phelps, Le Clos and Cseh by 0.75 seconds.

The swim earned Schooling S$1 million under Singapore's Multi-Million Dollar Award Programme, with 20 percent reinvested into the Singapore Swimming Association for youth development. The NCAA cleared the payment under regulations governing state rewards to foreign student-athletes. Upon his return, tens of thousands lined Singapore's streets for an open-top bus victory parade. Swimming outlet SwimSwam ranked the performance fourth on its list of the top swims of 2016, behind Katinka Hosszú, Katie Ledecky and Adam Peaty.

Adversity, National Service and Life After the Pool

Schooling completed his collegiate swimming career at Texas in 2017 with 12 NCAA titles (four individual and eight relays). At the 2017 Budapest World Championships, he claimed joint bronze in the 100m butterfly (50.83 seconds) behind Caeleb Dressel. He defended his 100m butterfly crown at the 2018 Jakarta Asian Games in 51.04 seconds and added the 50m butterfly title. However, technical adjustments, weight fluctuations and coaching transitions disrupted his preparation for the delayed Tokyo 2020 Olympics. In Tokyo in July 2021, Schooling finished 44th in the 100m butterfly heats with a time of 53.12 seconds, exiting in the preliminary round.

Personal loss followed four months later when his father Colin died of cancer on 18 November 2021 at age 73. In January 2022, Schooling enlisted for Singapore's mandatory National Service. In August 2022, he received an official censure from the Singapore National Olympic Council after admitting to consuming cannabis overseas while on leave during the Southeast Asian Games in Hanoi, resulting in the withdrawal of his sports training privileges for the remainder of his military term.

On 2 April 2024, at age 28, Schooling announced his retirement from competitive swimming. In business, he directs his academy, Swim Schooling, and operates as a founding partner at venture capital firm Swaen Schooling Capital alongside Cliff Go and Ben Ling. In 2025, the International Swimming Hall of Fame confirmed his induction as its first Singaporean member, capping a career that redefined Southeast Asian swimming.

item.title: From Heartbreak in London to History in Rio: The Life of Hoang Xuan Vinh
item.description: Overcoming childhood loss, severe nearsightedness and agonizing near-misses, the army officer delivered his country's first Olympic gold medal.
item.content:encoded:
On August 6, 2016, inside the Olympic Shooting Centre in Deodoro, Rio de Janeiro, 41-year-old military officer Hoang Xuan Vinh stood at firing point eight, trailing Brazilian shooter Felipe Almeida Wu by 0.2 points ahead of the twentieth and final shot of the men's 10-metre air pistol final. After Wu registered a 10.1 to ignite the home crowd, Xuan Vinh took several deep breaths, steadied his pistol, and delivered a 10.7 into the inner ring. The shot lifted his total to 202.5 points, established an Olympic record, and secured the first Olympic gold medal in the history of Vietnamese sports.

Four days later, Xuan Vinh added an Olympic silver medal in the 50-metre free pistol behind South Korea's Jin Jong-oh with a score of 191.3. That campaign in Brazil ended a 64-year Olympic medal drought for Vietnam, but the road to that podium was marked by family loss, material scarcity, and repeated competitive heartbreak.

The Barracks and a Late Calling

Born on October 6, 1974, in Son Tay, Xuan Vinh experienced tragedy early when his mother, a factory worker, died when he was three years old. His father, a soldier in the Vietnam People's Army, moved Xuan Vinh and his toddler sister into a small apartment in Hanoi, raising them on modest military wages. Following high school, Xuan Vinh enlisted in the armed forces, studying at the Military Engineering Officer School in Song Be province and training for nearly two years at Army Officer School 2.

Graduating in 1994, he received an assignment to the 239th Engineer Brigade in Thuong Tin, Ha Tay province. While performing his duties as an officer, his precision with military service rifles caught the attention of superiors during intra-army tournaments. In 1998, Xuan Vinh won first place at the national military shooting competition. The Army Club recruited him the following year, and at age 26 he transferred from active field command to join the national shooting programme. His late entrance into high-performance sport came alongside a physical handicap unusual for elite marksmen: Xuan Vinh competed while being severely nearsighted, using corrective shooting lenses to see the target.

Domestic and regional success followed quickly. In 1999, Xuan Vinh took bronze in the men's air pistol team event at the National Cup in Hai Phong. In 2000, the year he married Phan Huong Giang, he broke the national record in the 10-metre air pistol with 580 points to win national gold. Beginning at the 2001 Southeast Asian Games in Malaysia and running through the 2011 Games in Indonesia, Xuan Vinh captured at least one gold medal across six consecutive SEA Games editions, highlighted by a three-gold haul in Thailand in 2007.

Agony by One-Tenth of a Point

Despite regional dominance, Xuan Vinh's transition to world-level competition was haunted by late-round collapses. At the 2010 Asian Games in Guangzhou, he held first place in the men's 25-metre standard pistol before misfiring on his final shot during the rapid-fire stage, tumbling from the lead to 13th place.

Two years later, Xuan Vinh qualified for the 2012 London Olympics via the Asian Championship in Qatar. In London, he missed the 10-metre air pistol final by one point, finishing ninth with 582 points. In the 50-metre pistol final, Xuan Vinh entered the ninth shot needing only eight points to lock up an Olympic medal. He recorded a 7.3. Despite a 10.2 on his tenth shot for a 658.5 total, he missed the bronze medal by 0.1 points to China's Wang Zhiwei.

Devastated by the margin, Xuan Vinh contemplated retirement. Instead, national coach Nguyen Thi Nhung instituted an unorthodox regimen to harden his mental discipline. Before daily workouts, Xuan Vinh was required to shout aloud: "I am an Olympic medallist". To master stillness under pressure, he spent one full year practicing a routine of standing upright and motionless for two continuous hours without speaking. Training conditions in Hanoi remained tight, with Xuan Vinh often limited to 100 live rounds per day—a fraction of the ammunition used by rivals in Europe and East Asia. South Korean coach Park Chung-gun joined the coaching staff in late 2014, organizing overseas camps in South Korea so Xuan Vinh could practice on modern electronic scoring targets.

The changes bore fruit. In late 2012, Xuan Vinh won Vietnam's first Asian Air Gun Championship gold in China with 683.3 points. At the 2013 ISSF World Cup in Changwon, South Korea, he avenged his London loss by edging Wang Zhiwei with 200.8 points to claim Vietnam's first World Cup title.

Legacy Beyond Rio

Following his historic double-medal performance at Rio 2016, Xuan Vinh received promotion to the rank of colonel in the Vietnam People's Army and was voted Vietnam's Outstanding Athlete of 2016. He competed at his third Summer Games at the Tokyo Olympics in 2021, where he placed 22nd in the 10-metre air pistol qualifying round with 573 points.

After retiring from international competition, Colonel Xuan Vinh moved into coaching as the head coach of the Army Sports Shooting Team and an instructor within the national squad. In 2023, he stood behind the line at the 19th Asian Games in Hangzhou, China, guiding his pupil Pham Quang Huy to the men's 10-metre air pistol gold medal—Vietnam's first Asian Games shooting title in the event. Today, Xuan Vinh directs the Army shooting programme from Hanoi, mentoring junior military shooters pursuing qualification for future Olympic Games.

item.title: Tian Bingyi Appointed China Badminton Head Coach for Los Angeles 2028 Cycle
item.description: The 63-year-old former world champion takes the helm as two-time Olympic gold medallist Zhang Nan joins the national coaching setup.
item.content:encoded:
BEIJING — The Chinese Badminton Association (CBA) appointed veteran tactician Tian Bingyi as head coach of the Chinese national badminton team on Tuesday, November 24, 2026, placing the 63-year-old in charge of the country's preparations for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympic Games.

The decision was formally announced during the national squad's winter training mobilization conference in Beijing. Alongside Tian's appointment, the CBA confirmed that two-time Olympic champion Zhang Nan has joined the national coaching setup after serving as head coach of the Beijing municipal women's badminton team.

A unified helm for the road to Los Angeles

Tian's appointment marks a structural return to a unified head coaching role across China's national badminton program. In April 2017, the national setup had removed the singular head coach and deputy head coach titles, dividing technical leadership between singles head coach Xia Xuanze and doubles head coach Zhang Jun.

By installing Tian at the summit of the coaching hierarchy ahead of the 2028 Olympic cycle, the CBA aims to consolidate tournament preparations across all five disciplines. Tian brings decades of experience overseeing China's first team, second team, and junior squads through multiple Olympic Games, Asian Games, and World Championship campaigns.

Decades of championship pedigree

Born in Wuhan in July 1963, Tian built a distinguished career on the court before moving into coaching. Partnering Li Yongbo in men's doubles, Tian captured consecutive BWF World Championship titles in 1987 and 1989, earned bronze at the 1992 Barcelona Olympics, and helped China lift three straight Thomas Cup trophies in 1986, 1988, and 1990.

Following his competitive retirement after the 1992 Games, Tian took charge of China's national women's doubles group, mentoring Ge Fei and Gu Jun to back-to-back Olympic gold medals at Atlanta 1996 and Sydney 2000. He served as deputy head coach of the national team from 1997 to 2017 and was elected vice president of the Chinese Badminton Association in August 2023.

Olympic champion Zhang Nan bolsters staff

The coaching overhaul also integrates the elite experience of 36-year-old Zhang Nan. Zhang won Olympic gold in mixed doubles with Zhao Yunlei at London 2012 and men's doubles gold alongside Fu Haifeng at Rio 2016.

During his tenure as head coach of Beijing's women's team, Zhang guided the regional squad to titles and runner-up finishes at national tournaments. His transition into the senior national staff provides Tian with contemporary championship expertise as China begins its winter training block aimed at the 2028 Games.

item.title: Kamila Valieva Ruled Out of Russian Figure Skating Championships in Chelyabinsk
item.description: The 20-year-old was omitted from the preliminary entry list after doctors restricted her training workload following health issues.
item.content:encoded:
Kamila Valieva will not compete at the upcoming Russian Figure Skating Championships in Chelyabinsk, missing the country’s marquee domestic competition scheduled for Dec. 17–20. The 20-year-old was absent from the preliminary entry list released by the Figure Skating Federation of Russia (FFKKR) on Tuesday evening, confirming reports first published by Russian state news agencies TASS and RIA Novosti.

Valieva’s withdrawal follows an autumn disrupted by health concerns and training restrictions. In late October, medical staff advised the skater to suspend jumping elements for a month. While Valieva resumed on-ice practice on Nov. 12, team insiders told RIA Novosti that she has yet to return to full-intensity training routines required for national-level competition.

Medical setback halts autumn schedule

The training halt forced Valieva to skip the entire Russian Grand Prix circuit this season. She withdrew from the opening stage in Kazan on Oct. 17–18 due to illness and subsequently missed the series finale in Omsk on Nov. 14–15.

Valieva made her initial competitive return in January 2026 at the Russian jumping championships after completing a four-year suspension imposed by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) for a positive trimetazidine test dating back to December 2021. She skated in the national test skates in Moscow in September, but she has not contested a full two-program competitive event since the ban expired.

Coaching transition and eligibility shifts

The 2026–27 season has brought considerable structural changes for Valieva. After spending more than a year in Svetlana Sokolovskaia’s training group, she returned this autumn to the Khrustalny rink to work once again with veteran coach Eteri Tutberidze.

Her international status remains blocked. Although the International Skating Union (ISU) granted Valieva neutral athlete status in August, the governing body rescinded that designation in September.

Domestic figures acknowledged that Valieva’s absence represents a substantial blow to the tournament in Chelyabinsk. Renowned coach Alexander Zhulin told RIA Novosti that "the Russian championship will lose in spectacle due to her absence," while 1988 Olympic ice dance champion Natalia Bestemianova told TASS that Valieva "knows what she is doing, she has been through a lot" and must prioritize her health.

While Valieva sits out, the FFKKR’s preliminary field in Chelyabinsk features Beijing 2022 Olympic silver medalist Alexandra Ignatova (formerly Trusova) in the women's event, alongside a men's field headlined by Petr Gumennik and Vladislav Dikidzhi.

item.title: Bojan Hodak Appointed Malaysia Head Coach as Harimau Malaya Reorganise
item.description: The 55-year-old Croatian returns to Malaysian football as Tan Cheng Hoe transitions into the national team director role.
item.content:encoded:
PETALING JAYA — The Football Association of Malaysia (FAM) confirmed on Tuesday, November 24, 2026, the appointment of Bojan Hodak as the new head coach of the men's national team. The 55-year-old Croatian tactician succeeds interim head coach Tan Cheng Hoe, who took charge on June 25 following the departure of Peter Cklamovski. Cheng Hoe will now move into a full-time role as national team director.

A Proven Regional Track Record

Hodak brings two decades of coaching experience across Southeast Asian football, particularly in Malaysia. His most celebrated domestic run occurred in 2012, when he guided Kelantan to a domestic treble by capturing the Malaysia Super League, the FA Cup, and the Malaysia Cup.

He continued to accumulate domestic silverware across subsequent stints, steering Johor Darul Ta'zim to the 2014 Malaysia Super League title. Years later, he led Kuala Lumpur City FC to an unexpected triumph in the 2021 Malaysia Cup before guiding the capital club to the 2022 AFC Cup final, where they finished as runners-up.

item.title: From a Sweet Factory Court to Badminton History: The Life of Ratchanok Intanon
item.description: The 2013 world champion overcame poverty, chronic injuries and personal loss to remain Southeast Asia's defining singles shuttler.
item.content:encoded:
Ratchanok Intanon was born on 5 February 1995 in Yasothon province in northeastern Thailand, before moving to Bangkok with her parents, Winatthachai Intanon and Kamphan Suwannasara. Her parents took jobs as laborers at the Banthongyord sweet factory, where large vats of boiling syrup and sugar posed an everyday risk to children roaming the production floor. Factory owner Kamala Thongkorn stepped in to move six-year-old Ratchanok away from the machinery, guiding her onto the factory's private badminton courts so she could play safely while her parents worked. That decision formed the foundation of the Banthongyord Badminton School, where Chinese coach Xie Zhihua took charge of her daily technical education.

Nicknamed "May," Ratchanok won her first national junior tournament at age seven and made her international senior debut at 13 at the 2008 Laos International Series, reaching the women's singles final. In April 2009, at 14, she secured her maiden senior international title at the Vietnam International Challenge. Seven months later in Alor Setar, Malaysia, she defeated compatriot Porntip Buranaprasertsuk 21–15, 21–23, 21–10 to become the youngest-ever BWF World Junior champion. She proved that achievement was no anomaly by defending the world junior crown against Japan's Misaki Matsutomo in Guadalajara in 2010, and against Indonesia's Elyzabeth Purwaningtyas in Taoyuan in 2011, making her the first player to win three consecutive singles titles at the World Junior Championships.

The Breakthrough in Guangzhou and World Number One

Ratchanok stepped onto the senior global stage with a quarter-final run at the London 2012 Olympic Games at age 17, losing in three sets to China's second seed Wang Xin after taking the opening game. In March 2013, she reached the final of the All England Open in Birmingham, falling to Denmark's Tine Baun to become the tournament's youngest singles finalist. A month later, she defeated Germany's Juliane Schenk at the India Open to capture her maiden BWF Superseries title at 18 years, two months and 22 days.

Her defining triumph arrived on 11 August 2013 at the BWF World Championships in Guangzhou, China. Seeded fourth, she eliminated Spain's Carolina Marín in a three-game quarter-final and India's P. V. Sindhu in straight sets in the semi-finals. In the final, Ratchanok faced world number one and reigning Olympic champion Li Xuerui. In a 65-minute contest, Ratchanok recovered from deficits to defeat Li 22–20, 18–21, 21–14. At 18 years, six months and six days, she became the youngest singles world champion in badminton history and the first Thai shuttler to win a world championship title.

In April 2016, Ratchanok achieved an unprecedented physical run on the BWF circuit. Over three consecutive weeks, she won three straight Superseries titles: the India Open in New Delhi, the Malaysia Open in Shah Alam, and the Singapore Open, where she fought back to beat China's Sun Yu 18–21, 21–11, 21–14 in the final. The hat-trick lifted her to the women's singles world number one spot on 21 April 2016, making her the first Thai shuttler to top the BWF world rankings. Four months later, she served as Thailand's flag bearer at the 2016 Rio Olympic Games.

Heartbreak, Loss and the Drive to Keep Playing

Ratchanok's career at the highest level was continually tested by recurring knee, back and shoulder ailments. Yet she repeatedly rallied into form, winning the Asia Championships in Wuhan in 2015 by beating Li Xuerui in the final, and adding the Malaysia Masters titles in 2018 and 2019. At the delayed Tokyo Olympics in July 2021, she reached the quarter-finals before falling 21–14, 18–21, 18–21 to longtime rival Tai Tzu-ying of Chinese Taipei.

Just days after returning to Bangkok from Tokyo, Ratchanok suffered the deepest loss of her life. On 19 August 2021, her mother, Kamphan Suwannasara, suffered sudden respiratory failure. Ratchanok performed CPR at home, but her mother was pronounced dead on the way to the hospital. Devastated, Ratchanok withdrew from the Sudirman Cup and Uber Cup. When she eventually resumed training, she made a public vow to continue competing in memory of her mother.

She carried that motivation back onto the podium. In July 2022, Ratchanok defeated Olympic gold medalist Chen Yufei 21–15, 13–21, 21–16 to claim the Malaysia Open in Kuala Lumpur, dedicating the victory to her late mother. In March 2024, she ended another two-year title drought by winning the Spain Masters in Madrid, wearing a silver necklace containing a stone taken from her mother's home. "I choose one from her life, from her home, to take with me because she also never went overseas so now I take her everywhere," she told Olympics.com.

At the Paris 2024 Olympic Games, her fourth appearance at the Games, Ratchanok faced Tai Tzu-ying in their 36th career encounter during the group stage on 31 July. Ratchanok won 21–19, 21–15, and the two veterans shared a prolonged embrace and tears at the net. Ratchanok reached the quarter-finals at the Porte de la Chapelle Arena before losing to Indonesia's Gregoria Mariska Tunjung. Now in her late twenties, the shuttler who grew up alongside the sweet factory production lines continues to train at Banthongyord, anchoring Thailand's national team and honoring the promises that sustained her rise.

item.title: China U17 Earn First World Cup Point in 21 Years After 2-2 Morocco Draw
item.description: Striker Zhao Songyuan scored twice in Doha before a 99th-minute equalizer denied Satoshi Ukishima's side victory.
item.content:encoded:
The China under-17 national team earned their first point at the FIFA U-17 World Cup since 2005 after a 2-2 draw against Morocco in Doha on Monday, November 23, 2026. Striker Zhao Songyuan scored twice to give China a 2-0 lead before Morocco mounted a late comeback, sealing the draw with an equalizer in the ninth minute of second-half stoppage time.

Zhao ends 21-year goal drought

China entered the Group H fixture under pressure following a 5-0 loss to Spain in their tournament opener on November 20. Head coach Satoshi Ukishima made one change to his lineup, starting Pan Chaowei, and his side took the lead inside two minutes. Zhao intercepted a clearance in Morocco's half, drove past two defenders into the penalty area, and slid a low shot into the bottom corner. The strike was China's first goal at a men's U-17 World Cup in 21 years, dating back to Yang Xu's quarter-final goal against Turkey at Peru 2005.

Morocco, who reached the quarter-finals at both the 2023 and 2025 editions and brought a squad featuring 14 players based at European clubs, struggled to break down China's organized lines before the interval. In the 57th minute, China doubled their advantage on the counter-attack. Winger He Sifan delivered a cross from the right flank, allowing the 1.94-metre Zhao to arrive inside the six-yard box and turn the ball home for his second goal of the match.

Morocco's stoppage-time equalizer

The momentum shifted in the 64th minute when Chinese defender Nan Zixun committed a pulling foul inside the penalty area. Morocco forward Ziyad Baha converted the spot-kick to reduce the deficit to 2-1. Morocco subsequently pinned China back into their own half, culminating in the 99th minute when Loghmani turned home a close-range rebound to level the score.

"I was very happy to help the team with two goals, but we could not hold onto our advantage," Zhao said after the match. "Conceding at the very end was really regrettable". Ukishima gathered the squad on the pitch immediately following the final whistle. "The players executed the plan well against individual quality, but we dropped into a defensive mindset too early and lost concentration at the end," Ukishima said.

Fiji finale decides Group H fate

The result leaves Spain atop Group H with six points after a 15-0 victory over Fiji on Monday. Morocco sit second on four points with a plus-six goal difference, while China are third with one point and a minus-five goal difference. Fiji remain fourth with zero points and 21 goals conceded across two matches.

With the expanded 48-team tournament featuring 12 groups, the top two finishers in each pool and the eight best third-placed teams qualify for the Round of 32. China conclude their Group H schedule against Fiji on Thursday, November 26, in Doha, where a victory is required to keep their knockout qualification hopes alive.

The six-day competition runs from 28 November to 3 December at the Martial Arts Arena in Tashkent's Olympic Village. A total of 142 boxers from 31 nations will contest 20 weight categories—ten for men and ten for women—with brackets capped at eight competitors per division following qualification stages earlier this year in Brazil and China.

Youth champions and veteran leadership

Three-time World Championship medallist and Paris 2024 Olympian Karina Ibragimova headlines the Kazakh women's selection at 57kg. The Tashkent tournament renews the long-standing ring rivalry between Kazakhstan and host nation Uzbekistan, who entered an 18-boxer delegation that features men's 80kg world champion Javokhir Ummataliev and heavyweight Jahongir Zokirov.

Kazakhstan enjoyed strong momentum across the 2026 World Boxing Cup circuit. item.title: Russian Boxing Federation Voted In as Full World Boxing Member in Panama
item.description: Delegates at the fourth annual World Boxing Congress approve full voting rights for Russia as the Olympic governing body expands ahead of LA 2028.
item.content:encoded:
The Russian Boxing Federation has become a full member of World Boxing following a majority vote by delegates at the international body's fourth annual Congress in Panama City on 20 November 2026.

The decision grants Russia official voting rights under World Boxing's "one country, one vote" constitutional principle at future general assemblies. Andrei Istomin, Deputy General Secretary of the Russian Boxing Federation, represented the delegation in Panama under instructions from General Secretary Alexander Besputin.

"The most important result for us was the admission of the Russian Boxing Federation into World Boxing as a full member, which the majority of countries voted for," Istomin said.

The Shift from Endorsed to Full Status

Russia's accession to full status completes an eight-month procedural transition. World Boxing initially accepted the Russian Boxing Federation's application in March 2026 as an endorsed member without voting privileges.

The vote in Panama was part of a broader expansion, with the Congress approving applications from 47 national federations to lift the governing body to 170 full voting members and one associate member.

World Boxing President Gennadiy Golovkin, the former unified world middleweight champion from Kazakhstan who oversees the federation, addressed the assembly following the votes.

"Today marked another important milestone for World Boxing and the future of our sport," Golovkin said. "The decisions made by our member federations confirm our shared commitment to putting boxers first, strengthening our organisation, and doing everything possible to ensure boxing continues to develop as a credible and respected Olympic sport. I am particularly pleased that our members supported the course we have set leading up to the 2028 Olympic Games in Los Angeles and beyond."

Governance and the Road to LA28

World Boxing was founded in April 2023 by member associations seeking an alternative international federation capable of securing the sport's long-term future in the Olympic programme following the International Olympic Committee's de-recognition of the International Boxing Association (IBA).

Full membership integrates Russia into World Boxing's governance structure, committee appointments and constitutional ballots. Russian coaching council chairman Eduard Kravtsov told Match TV that full status normalises the country's position: "We were non-full members in World Boxing, and for Russia that was unacceptable. Everything has fallen into place."

While full membership formalises Russia's standing inside the governing body, Olympic qualifying events under World Boxing oversight are scheduled to begin in 2027 as the sport prepares for the 2028 Games in Los Angeles.

item.title: Mirra Andreeva Earns $10.65 Million to Enter Global Top Five in 2026 Prize Money
item.description: The 19-year-old French Open champion finished second among female players, trailing only Kazakhstan's Elena Rybakina in Sportico's year-end rankings.
item.content:encoded:
Russian 19-year-old Mirra Andreeva generated $10.65 million in prize money during the 2026 tennis season, placing fifth across all players worldwide in financial rankings published by Sportico on November 23. The world No. 2 finished behind only Kazakhstan’s world No. 1 Elena Rybakina among female players, joining three ATP stars atop the combined tour earnings list.

Germany’s Alexander Zverev led all players in the 2026 calculations with $18.18 million, supported by men's singles titles at the French Open and the US Open. Carlos Alcaraz finished second with $12.55 million following his title run at the ATP Finals in Turin, while Wimbledon champion Jannik Sinner placed third at $11.61 million. Rybakina secured fourth overall and led the WTA Tour with $11.13 million, leaving Andreeva fifth at $10.65 million.

Roland Garros triumph anchors Andreeva's rise

Andreeva, born in Krasnoyarsk, compiled a tour-leading 55 singles victories across 71 matches during 2026. Her season featured four WTA singles titles, highlighted by her first Grand Slam singles championship at Roland Garros and an undefeated title run at the WTA Finals.

The $10.65 million purse marked a sharp acceleration in Andreeva's career on-court compensation. After collecting $25,811 in 2022, she took home $750,477 in 2023, $1.92 million in 2024, and $4.7 million in 2025 before crossing the eight-figure barrier in her second full year as a senior top-10 competitor.

Central Asian and global milestones

Rybakina's $11.13 million haul established the highest single-season prize total recorded by a tennis player representing Kazakhstan. Her season included Grand Slam victories at the Australian Open and the US Open, alongside WTA tournament titles in Stuttgart and Ningbo.

Aryna Sabalenka finished sixth overall on the combined leaderboard with $8.61 million. Ben Shelton of the United States and Linda Noskova of the Czech Republic followed in a tie for seventh at $8.29 million each. Coco Gauff ranked ninth with $7.76 million, and Jessica Pegula placed 10th with $6.47 million.

Russian men's No. 1 Daniil Medvedev finished 13th overall with $5.66 million, sitting between Ukraine's Elina Svitolina ($6.15 million), Czech finalist Karolina Muchova ($5.67 million), and Italian semifinalist Flavio Cobolli ($5.31 million). Frances Tiafoe rounded out the top 15 with $5.21 million. Andreeva and Rybakina are scheduled to open their 2027 campaigns in Australia in January as the top two seeds for the Australian Open in Melbourne.

item.title: Kun Khmer champion Chhut Serey Vannthong outpoints Riki at K-1 Revenge II in Tokyo
item.description: The Cambodian won all three scorecards at Korakuen Hall, the latest Kun Khmer fighter to make his mark in K-1's super-featherweight division
item.content:encoded:
Cambodian Kun Khmer champion Chhut Serey Vannthong beat Japan's Riki on Monday, 23 November, by unanimous decision at K-1 Revenge II at Korakuen Hall in Tokyo. The judges scored the three-round super-featherweight (-60 kg) bout 30-27, 30-28 and 30-28.

The 26-year-old from Battambang came to Tokyo as the ISKA Kun Khmer Intercontinental super-featherweight (-59 kg) champion, with a record of 84 wins (33 by knockout), 13 defeats and 3 draws, according to Japanese magazine Gong Kakutogi. He also won Kun Khmer gold at the 2023 SEA Games in Phnom Penh. Both fighters made weight the day before: Riki at 59.7 kg and Chhut at 59.9 kg.

How the fight was won

Chhut set the pattern early with his kicks. In the first round he threw repeated left kicks, then used right low kicks and calf kicks to unsettle Riki's stance, switching to the body with his left leg. Riki, a karate-trained fighter from K-1 Gym Meguro Team Tiger, answered with right hooks and front kicks.

Riki pressed forward with his jab in the second round, but Chhut kept scoring with body kicks, straight rights and a jumping knee. In the third, the Cambodian landed a left body kick and a right knee early, made Riki dip with a punch that the referee ruled a slip, and finished the fight with a straight right and a right uppercut. There were no knockdowns, but the cards showed a clear win.

At the weigh-in the day before, Chhut kept his message short: "My opponent is strong, but I want to win for myself."

The third Kun Khmer fighter to make an impact

Chhut was announced as K-1's third Kun Khmer challenger of the year. In September, Lorn Panha beat Japan's Kazuki Matsumoto at K-1 World MAX 2026 to reach the World MAX final tournament, where he meets Zack Pankhurst in the quarter-finals in Yokohama on 29 December. Thun Menghong also gave Japan's Tomoya Yokoyama a hard fight in a bout Japanese media described as fierce.

Chhut's win now puts a Cambodian fighter in K-1's super-featherweight picture. Yokoyama holds the K-1 interim super-featherweight (-60 kg) title, which he won with a first-round knockout of Yuta Matsuyama on 31 May.

What comes next

K-1 has not yet announced Chhut's next fight. A win over an established Japanese fighter, scored clearly by all three judges, is the kind of result that usually earns a step up in opposition, and Cambodian fans are already hoping it leads to a title opportunity. For now, Chhut returns home as the latest proof that Kun Khmer fighters can win under K-1 rules, which ban elbows and limit clinching, two of Kun Khmer's main weapons.

item.title: Trefilov Rejects 2028 Olympic Medal Guarantee by Russian Handball Chief
item.description: The 2016 Rio gold medal coach cautions against bold podium pledges as officials pursue a wild card path to Los Angeles.
item.content:encoded:
Former Russian women's national handball coach Yevgeni Trefilov dismissed public guarantees of an Olympic podium finish at Los Angeles 2028, telling newspaper Sport-Express on Sunday, 22 November 2026, that "money loves silence, and victories do too". His comments directly addressed statements made two days earlier by Sergey Shishkarev, chairman of the Supreme Council of the Handball Federation of Russia (HFR), who vowed that the national squad would medal when the Games take place in July 2028.

"The chances are always 50-50. I wouldn't get so hot-headed," the 71-year-old Trefilov said to Sport-Express. "Everything should be done quietly. As they say, money loves silence, and victories do too. Of course, I would like to see our national team on the podium all the time. It is very pleasant and warms the soul".

Contrasting Visions at Moscow Film Premiere

The exchange followed the premiere of the documentary film Miracle in Rio (Chudo v Rio), directed by Nikolai Akelkin, held in Moscow on Friday, 20 November 2026. The documentary chronicles Russia’s run to the gold medal at the 2016 Rio de Janeiro Olympics, where Trefilov coached the squad to a 22-19 victory over France in the final after an overtime semifinal win against Norway featuring decisive penalty conversions by Ekaterina Ilyina.

Speaking at the screening, Shishkarev projected a return to the Olympic rostrum: "There is a specific date — July 2028, the city is Los Angeles. I promise you that the Russian national team will stand on the podium there". Trefilov struck a more reserved tone from the same stage on Friday. "We talk a lot and do little. Victory is just a moment. After a victory, you need to go back to the gym for another second of victory," Trefilov said. "I would like handball to be treated a little differently. Our girls showed with their results at the Olympics that handball is not the last sport for Russia".

The Hurdles Facing Los Angeles 2028

Russia captured women's handball gold at Rio 2016 and followed it with silver at Tokyo 2020, but the national side has not contested an Olympic fixture since August 2021 following international bans from world and European competitions instituted in 2022. The 2028 Summer Olympic Games in Los Angeles are scheduled to run from 14 to 30 July 2028, leaving a narrow qualification window.

To establish a qualification route, Russian officials are seeking entry into the 2027 IHF Women's World Championship. Shishkarev confirmed plans to hold talks with International Handball Federation (IHF) president Hassan Moustafa to request a wild card invitation for the Russian team, which would allow them to compete for the Olympic tournament berths awarded at the event.

item.title: Vietnam Earn Historic First U17 World Cup Point in 3-3 Thriller Against New Zealand
item.description: Cristiano Roland's squad fought back three times before Trương Nguyễn Duy Khang headed a 92nd-minute equalizer in Doha.
item.content:encoded:
Vietnam’s under-17 men's national football team earned their first point in FIFA U-17 World Cup history on Monday, November 23, 2026, rallying three separate times to secure a 3-3 draw against New Zealand at the Aspire Zone in Doha, Qatar.

Substitute Trương Nguyễn Duy Khang scored the decisive equalizer in the 92nd minute, heading home after New Zealand goalkeeper Joseph Chalabi parried an initial delivery into the penalty area. The Oceania champions nearly snatched victory two minutes later when midfielder Joe McIntyre struck the goalpost from distance in the 94th minute.

Three deficits erased in Doha

New Zealand opened the scoring in the 19th minute of the Group G fixture when forward Jack Clegg converted from close range following a low cross from Matias Nunez. The Vietnamese side trailed 1-0 at half-time despite registering several dangerous attempts on goal.

Head coach Cristiano Roland’s side leveled four minutes into the second half. Midfielder Chu Ngọc Nguyễn Lực curled a direct free-kick from the left wing into the bottom corner in the 49th minute. New Zealand restored their advantage three minutes later when James Wenceslao delivered a cross from the right flank, allowing John Woldegiorgis to head past Vietnamese goalkeeper Lý Xuân Hòa in the 52nd minute.

Vietnam equalized again in the 58th minute. Nguyễn Lực split the New Zealand defense with a through ball to Lê Trọng Đại Nhân, who finished past Chalabi. The assistant referee initially raised an offside flag, but Vietnam's coaching staff requested a review under FIFA's Football Video Support (FVS) protocol, prompting the referee to overturn the call and award the goal. New Zealand capitalized on a set piece to take their third lead in the 66th minute when captain Ethan Dyer powered in a header from a corner kick.

First point keeps qualification alive

Duy Khang’s stoppage-time header secured Vietnam's breakthrough point at a global FIFA tournament following their opening 3-2 defeat against European runners-up Belgium on November 20. New Zealand also picked up their first point of the campaign after losing 3-0 to Mali in their opener.

The result leaves Vietnam third in Group G with one point and a minus-one goal difference. Mali top the standings with six points after defeating Belgium, who sit second on three points. New Zealand occupy fourth place with one point and a minus-three goal difference. Under the 48-team tournament structure in Qatar, the top two teams in each group advance to the round of 32 alongside the eight best third-placed finishers.

Vietnam finish their group schedule on Thursday, November 26, 2026, when they face Mali at the Aspire Zone.

item.title: Carlos Alcaraz Defeats Alexander Zverev in Turin to Claim Maiden ATP Finals Title
item.description: The 23-year-old Spaniard joins Agassi, Federer and Djokovic as the fourth man to win all four Grand Slams and the year-end championship.
item.content:encoded:
What happened

On Sunday, 22 November 2026, Carlos Alcaraz defeated world No. 1 Alexander Zverev 6-2, 7-6 (9-7) in the final of the Nitto ATP Finals at the Inalpi Arena in Turin. The 23-year-old Spaniard broke Zverev's serve four times during a match that lasted two hours and one minute. In the second-set tiebreak, Zverev erased an early deficit to create three set points, but Alcaraz erased all three before converting his second championship point with a backhand winner to claim the season-ending trophy for the first time in his career.

Why it is being talked about

The victory makes Alcaraz only the fourth male player in tennis history to win all four Grand Slam tournaments and the ATP Finals, joining Andre Agassi, Roger Federer and Novak Djokovic. At 23 years of age, he is the youngest man to complete that combination of titles. The outcome in Turin also delivered an emphatic conclusion to the 2026 season: while Zverev won Roland Garros and the US Open to finish the year ranked world No. 1, Alcaraz defeated him head-to-head in the season finale. "You are an absolute legend of our sport, and you are only 23," Zverev told Alcaraz during the trophy ceremony.

Key facts and numbers

Alcaraz went through the tournament with an undefeated 5-0 match record, dropping only a single set across wins over Frances Tiafoe, Daniil Medvedev, Flavio Cobolli, Ben Shelton and Zverev. By finishing unbeaten, the Spaniard collected a record payout of $5.171 million from the event's $15.75 million prize pool, along with 1,500 ATP ranking points.

The trophy was Alcaraz's 30th career tour-level singles title and his sixth of 2026, adding to autumn tournament wins in Tokyo, Vienna and the Paris Masters. Alcaraz concluded his 2026 campaign with a 47-5 win-loss record despite missing four and a half months during the spring and summer because of a right wrist injury. Zverev finished his year with a 69-win record, 10,320 points and the year-end No. 1 ranking.

What happens next

The ATP Tour now enters its brief winter off-season before the 2027 calendar begins in Australia in January. Alcaraz finishes 2026 ranked world No. 3, trailing world No. 2 Jannik Sinner by 350 points and Zverev at the top of the standings. Sinner, who missed the Turin finale with a knee injury scheduled for surgery on 24 November, is expected to return alongside Alcaraz and Zverev for the Australian Open.

item.title: Manny Pacquiao: The Street Fighter Who Conquered Eight Divisions
item.description: From sleeping on Manila pavements to winning belts across four decades, the Filipino icon built an unmatched legacy.
item.content:encoded:
Before Manny Pacquiao became the only eight-division champion in boxing history, he stood on construction sites in Manila at age 14, weighing less than 100 pounds and deciding whether his spare coins should purchase food or be mailed back to his mother in General Santos.

That struggle defined one of the most remarkable careers in world sport. Over a professional journey spanning three decades and 73 bouts, Pacquiao compiled a record of 62 wins, eight defeats and two draws, claiming 12 major world championships and becoming the only boxer to capture titles across four separate calendar decades.

The Dirt Rings of General Santos

Emmanuel Dapidran Pacquiao was born on December 17, 1978, in Kibawe, Bukidnon, before his family relocated to General Santos in South Cotabato. He was the fourth of six children born to Rosalio Pacquiao and Dionisia Dapidran. When his parents separated during his sixth-grade school year, the household plunged into deep financial distress. Pacquiao completed his primary education at Saavedra Saway Elementary School, but crippling household poverty forced him to leave formal schooling behind as a teenager.

His path shifted in February 1990. At 11 years old, Pacquiao watched 42-to-1 underdog James "Buster" Douglas knock out undisputed heavyweight champion Mike Tyson in Tokyo. His maternal uncle, Sardo Mejia, noticed the boy's fascination and constructed a makeshift gym in a home backyard. Six months later, Pacquiao was competing in public park fights in General Santos, earning small cash prizes that bought sacks of rice.

By 15, he had established himself as the top amateur junior in Mindanao, compiling a 60–4 amateur record. Seeking greater competition and income to support his family, he boarded a boat to Manila as a stowaway, working day jobs on building sites and sleeping in boxing gyms before making his paid debut in January 1995 as a 106-pound junior flyweight at age 16.

Conquering Eight Divisions

Pacquiao claimed his first world championship on December 4, 1998, knocking out Chatchai Sasakul in Thailand to capture the WBC flyweight title just two weeks shy of his 20th birthday. Yet it was his move to the United States in 2001, pairing with trainer Freddie Roach at the Wild Card Gym in Hollywood, that triggered his meteoric rise.

Stepping in on two weeks' notice in June 2001, Pacquiao stopped IBF super bantamweight champion Lehlohonolo Ledwaba in Las Vegas. Over the next decade, his hand speed and southpaw angles dismantled a generation of future Hall of Famers. He stopped Marco Antonio Barrera in 2003, engaged in a celebrated trilogy with Érik Morales, and contested four dramatic bouts against Mexican rival Juan Manuel Márquez.

As Pacquiao added muscle without sacrificing punching speed, he shattered conventional limits on weight climbing. In December 2008, he moved up two divisions to dismantle Oscar De La Hoya, forcing the boxing superstar to retire on his stool after eight rounds. Five months later, in May 2009, he knocked Ricky Hatton unconscious in round two at the MGM Grand to capture the Ring light welterweight crown.

By the time he punished Antonio Margarito over 12 brutal rounds for the WBC super welterweight belt in November 2010, Pacquiao had secured world titles across eight distinct weight classes—a feat unmatched in boxing annals. He captured lineal championships in four weight categories (flyweight, featherweight, super featherweight and light welterweight), and collected belts in four of the sport's original divisions.

Longevity remained his signature trademark. In July 2019, at 40 years and seven months old, Pacquiao handed Keith Thurman his first professional defeat in Las Vegas, capturing the WBA welterweight crown to become the oldest welterweight titleholder in boxing history.

Life Beyond the Ropes

Outside the ring, Pacquiao transformed his fame into business ventures and civic leadership. He earned his secondary school equivalency diploma in February 2007 before entering public office. Voters in Sarangani elected him to the Philippine House of Representatives in 2010, where he served two terms before winning a nationwide seat in the Philippine Senate in 2016.

Between legislative sessions and world title camps, he played and coached in the Philippine Basketball Association for Kia from 2014 to 2017, later founding the semi-professional Maharlika Pilipinas Basketball League. In music, his recording of "Sometimes When We Touch" climbed to number 19 on the US Billboard Adult Contemporary chart.

Pacquiao retired from boxing in September 2021 to mount a campaign for the Philippine presidency, finishing third in the May 2022 election won by Ferdinand Marcos Jr. After stepping back from electoral contests following the 2025 midterm cycle, Marcos named him head of the National Anti-Poverty Commission in 2026—bringing the former street laborer full circle to address the systemic deprivation that first sent him into a boxing ring.

item.title: Svay Rieng and Phnom Penh Crown chase a historic AFC Champions League Two double
item.description: Svay Rieng arrive top of the Cambodian Premier League after a 5-0 win, while group leaders Crown carry poor league form into a decisive trip to Kuching
item.content:encoded:
Cambodia's two clubs in the AFC Champions League Two go into Thursday's fifth round of group matches, on 26 November, in very different moods. Preah Khan Reach Svay Rieng top the Cambodian Premier League (CPL) after a 5-0 win over Angkor Tiger on Sunday. Phnom Penh Crown lead their Asian group but sit eighth at home after a 1-1 draw with Kirivong Sok Sen Chey on Saturday.

With two group matches left for each side, both clubs can still reach the Round of 16 in February.

Svay Rieng: in form at the right time

Svay Rieng have scored nine goals and conceded one in four days. On 19 November they beat Thailand's Port FC 4-1 in the ASEAN Club Championship, with goals from Min Ratanak, Martins Júnior, Tiago Alves and Kwame Peprah. On Sunday they beat Angkor Tiger 5-0 in front of 7,502 spectators, more than three-quarters of the 9,789 who watched the five Week 8 matches.

The three-time defending champions are unbeaten after seven league games (five wins, two draws), with the league's best attack (22 goals) and best defence (5 conceded). They lead on 17 points, level with Nagaworld, who have played a game more.

In Group G of the AFC Champions League Two, Svay Rieng are second on 7 points. They lost 2-0 away to Japan's FC Machida Zelvia, drew 0-0 at home with Shanghai Shenhua, won 5-1 away to Singapore's Tampines Rovers and beat Tampines 2-0 at home.

Machida, who have won all four games, now visit Cambodia on Thursday. The top two in each group go through. Svay Rieng lead Shenhua by three points, and the two sides meet in the final round, so any point against Machida would take Svay Rieng into that last match with an advantage. The one concern is fatigue: Thursday is their third match in eight days.

Phnom Penh Crown: strong in Asia, struggling at home

Crown are a different team on each stage. In Group H they lead with 9 points from four games: a 2-1 win over Malaysia's Kuching City, a 2-1 win away to Korea's Gangwon FC, a 2-0 home win over Hong Kong's Kitchee and a 2-1 defeat in the return match in Hong Kong. Kitchee are second on 5 points, with Kuching and Gangwon on 4.

A win in Kuching on Thursday would give Crown 12 points, more than any other team in the group can reach, and confirm first place with a game to spare.

At home, the record eight-time champions have one league win in seven matches (one win, four draws, two defeats) and sit eighth on 7 points, ten behind Svay Rieng. Their only victory was 2-1 away to the Royal Cambodian Armed Forces on 24 October. In November they lost 1-0 to MOI Kompong Dewa and 2-1 to Boeung Ket before Saturday's draw with Kirivong, who are tenth. With only the top two earning continental places for next season, Crown cannot let the gap grow much further.

The title race: Nagaworld and Visakha keep pace

Nagaworld have matched the leaders on points. A 1-0 win over ISI Dangkor Senchey on Saturday took them level with Svay Rieng on 17 points from eight games. Their only league defeat was a 3-1 loss at Svay Rieng on 8 November, and their goal difference (+4) is far smaller than the leaders' (+17), showing how many of their wins have been narrow.

Visakha, seventh last season, are third on 16 points from seven games and had no match in Week 8. They have scored 19 goals, second only to Svay Rieng. Andrés Nieto, the Colombian-born Cambodia international who joined from Crown, scored twice in a 6-1 win away to the Royal Cambodian Armed Forces. Visakha drew 2-2 at Svay Rieng on 24 October, and their only defeat was a 3-1 loss at Angkor Tiger on 8 November.

MOI Kompong Dewa are fourth on 13 points after a 2-1 win on Sunday, with the league's second-best defence (5 conceded in seven games).

At the bottom: no points for the Royal Cambodian Armed Forces

The Royal Cambodian Armed Forces (National Defense), who reverted to that name in 2025, have lost all seven league games. They have scored 7 goals and conceded 29. Their defeats include 4-0 at Svay Rieng, 6-0 at Angkor Tiger and 6-1 at home to Visakha. The closest they came was a 5-4 home defeat to Nagaworld in September. Sunday's 2-1 home loss to MOI Kompong Dewa left them eight points behind tenth-placed Kirivong Sok Sen Chey.

item.title: Bangladesh and Singapore finalize preparations ahead of December women's friendlies
item.description: Interim coach Eric Mare leads Dhaka camp while Lionesses name Umairah Hamdan captain for two-match series
item.content:encoded:
The Bangladesh women's national football team began the final phase of their preparations in Dhaka on Sunday, 22 November 2026, ahead of a two-match international friendly series away against Singapore.

French coach Eric Mare, appointed by the Bangladesh Football Federation on a one-month contract while permanent head coach Peter Butler receives medical treatment in England, directed Sunday's session at the National Stadium. The squad had returned to Dhaka on 20 November after completing a three-week residential camp that began on 31 October at the Korean Export Processing Zone in Anwara, Chattogram. The camp featured veteran midfielders Maria Manda and Ritu Porna Chakma, defender Afida Khandaker, and 17-year-old Australian-born trialist Tazara Khan.

Ishida hands armband to Umairah

Singapore head coach Mihoko Ishida finalized a 28-player roster on 20 November, appointing 24-year-old Lion City Sailors defender Umairah Hamdan as captain. Umairah, who holds 36 international caps, led Singapore at the AFF Women's Cup in July, where a third-place finish secured qualification for the 2027 ASEAN Women's Championship.

"At the AFF Women's Cup, she always communicated the team's ideas clearly and played a very important role for us," Ishida said of Umairah. The Lionesses squad features uncapped overseas prospects including So Cal Blues defender Kylie Loo and IMG Academy midfielder Aria Romano, alongside recalls for forward Lila Tan and midfielder Raudhah Kamis. Singapore midfielder Putri Syaliza also returned to the national setup after receiving medical clearance ahead of her pending move to Australian club West Torrens Birkalla.

Head-to-head record and schedule

Bangladesh occupy 106th place in the FIFA Women's World Ranking, while Singapore sit 151st. Bangladesh have won all three previous meetings between the nations without conceding a goal. In their first meeting in 2017, Bangladesh won 2-0 in Singapore. The sides met again in Dhaka in December 2023, where Bangladesh recorded 3-0 and 8-0 victories.

Bangladesh will depart Dhaka for Singapore on 29 November. The first friendly takes place behind closed doors at Bishan Stadium on Tuesday, 1 December. The second encounter will follow on Saturday, 5 December at Jalan Besar Stadium in front of spectators, with both games kicking off at 7:30 pm local time and counting toward the FIFA rankings. For Singapore, the matches serve as preparation for the 2027 ASEAN Women's Championship in April and the 34th Southeast Asian Games in Malaysia in September 2027.
